title: Top 5 School Chromebook Dangers: How Students Access Inappropriate Content
author: CAL
summary: This guest essay on Emily Cherkin's newsletter is written by a paraprofessional technician (CAL) in a Northern California district that uses Lightspeed classroom-monitoring software on school Chromebooks. He reports what the monitoring shows students reaching despite filters: sexual content surfaced through Google Search and its AI Overview, unrestricted Reddit, violent and sexualized YouTube material (including a Google Slides route around a YouTube block), AI image generators that produce sexualized images, and adult sites posing as academic ones. He argues that filters tend to block by site name, so look-alike domains slip through, and that students share workarounds. His conclusion is that any internet-connected Chromebook means potential access to inappropriate content and that districts and parents must decide what to do with that reality. Cherkin frames the piece with a note that she asked him to write it after he contacted her, and he is identified only by initials.
points: District monitoring software reveals both what students can reach and how they bypass filters, which few parents, teachers, administrators or board members see.
Filters often judge sites by name, so obviously explicit domains are blocked while sites posing as academic platforms stay open.
A blocked YouTube can still be reached through Google Slides' insert-video feature using a school Gmail login.
AI image tools and Google's AI Overview add risks beyond plagiarism, including sexualized images of classmates and step-by-step explicit instructions.
The author concludes that no fully effective guardrail exists while Chromebooks and open internet access remain in classrooms.
quotes: Like other school districts in America, our district in California has Chromebooks in every classroom.

We have been using Lightspeed for two semesters to monitor the URL history and screen activity of our classrooms. Lightspeed allows us to see not only what inappropriate content students can access but how they are able to access it.
It is true that YouTube will blur explicit images, but YouTube also contains endless videos that show students how to turn off blur and how to watch age-restricted content.
After asking the AI platform if the more explicit image was appropriate to present to the class, the AI admitted it was not. But that did not prevent it from creating the image.
When school districts discuss “using AI responsibly,” plagiarism and academic integrity are not the only concerns that should be discussed.
In our experience tracking students’ URL history and screen activity, we’ve discovered that whether a Chromebook blocks or allows access to certain websites all depends on the website’s name.
Despite all of my school’s efforts to block access to inappropriate content, students have found countless ways of bypassing filters.
But as long as Google Chromebooks are allowed in the classroom, we can never guarantee that our children are safe.
